solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Distraught spouse in pieces

indicators.note: someone distraught is all over the place, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A grief-stricken husband or wife who has fallen to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In pieces' looks like it describes the distraught spouse, but 'in' is only a joiner and 'pieces' is the definition: OPUSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical or literary pieces are works, and opuses is the plural of opus, a composer's numbered work.

clue.text: Balance underpins diving position for swimmer

indicators.note: in a down entry, what underpins something sits beneath it, so this piece comes second

blocks.note: the pike is a diving position with the body bent at the hips and legs straight
to perch is to balance on a narrow support

explanation.surface: A diver's poise is the foundation of a good pike position, as a swimming coach might say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' suggests a person in the pool, but it is a fish; PIKEPERCH is itself made of two fish names.
explanation.definitionFit: The pikeperch is a European freshwater fish, the zander, and any fish can be called a swimmer in crosswords.

clue.text: Element of reportedly foolish trick

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: foolish is silly and a trick is a con; say the pair together

explanation.surface: Part of a supposedly stupid prank, as someone has told it.
explanation.walkthrough: SILLY CON spoken quickly gives SILICON, element 14.
explanation.definitionFit: Silicon is a chemical element, the semiconductor used in computer chips, with atomic number fourteen.

clue.text: Falter, cutting long story short

indicators.note: to cut something is to trim it down, so a letter is removed
something that falls short is incomplete, missing its final part

blocks.note: a saga is a long, rambling tale

explanation.surface: Someone stumbling as they try to abbreviate a rambling anecdote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting a long story short' is an everyday idiom; here it literally docks the last letter of SAGA to leave SAG.
explanation.definitionFit: To sag is to weaken or lose momentum, as when spirits or sales flag and begin to decline.

clue.text: Grand gold box is most ungainly

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a chest is a large box

explanation.surface: A huge, ornate golden casket is the clumsiest piece in the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand gold box' reads as one ornate object, but each word gives its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Gauche means socially awkward or clumsy, so the superlative describes whoever is the clumsiest of all.

clue.text: Clobber sheep behind empty garage

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its insides, leaving only the outer letters
being behind means coming after, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
a tup is a ram, a male sheep

explanation.surface: Someone told to beat a sheep found loitering behind a cleared-out garage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks like a verb meaning hit, but it is British slang for clothes or gear. TUP is a common crossword ram.
explanation.definitionFit: A get-up is an outfit, often an odd one, and clobber is British slang for clothing or belongings.

clue.text: Ben perhaps entering bus lane, busy beyond words

indicators.note: a busy scene is chaotic and bustling, so these letters are jumbled
entering means going inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged
a ben is a Scottish mountain, as in Ben Nevis; 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a peak

explanation.surface: A man called Ben pulling into a bus lane during a hectic rush hour, causing indescribable chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ben' reads as a driver's name but is a Scottish mountain, Ben Nevis being the best known. The rearranged letters split into two parts so the mountain can sit inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unspeakable is too awful to be expressed, literally impossible to put into speech.

clue.text: Unfortunate orphan pierced by old spear

indicators.note: something unfortunate has gone wrong, so these letters are knocked out of order
a thing pierced has something driven into it, so a piece goes inside

blocks.note: six letters to rearrange
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A luckless orphan run through with an ancient spear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pierced' suits the spear in the surface, but it is the instruction to drive the old letter into the rearranged word.
explanation.definitionFit: A harpoon is a barbed spear thrown or fired to catch whales and large fish.

clue.text: Charming university dons watch the pennies

indicators.note: to don is to put on, as clothing, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: to watch the pennies is to be thrifty
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Smooth-talking academics who are careful with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university lecturers, which suits 'university', but it is the verb: SAVE puts on U.
explanation.definitionFit: Suave describes someone smoothly polished and gracious in manner, an urbane and charming person.

clue.text: “Discontented” kiddy breaking fragile window

indicators.note: without its contents a word keeps only its outer letters
breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: slight means frail or delicate
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A sulky child smashes a delicate pane of glass.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'Discontented' carry no wordplay; they make the surface read as a description of a grumpy child.
explanation.definitionFit: A skylight is a window set into a roof or ceiling to let daylight in from above.

clue.text: Society elite laugh wildly

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for society
the cream is the best, the top layer of a group

explanation.surface: High society's grandees roaring with laughter at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Society elite' reads as one phrase, but splits into an abbreviation and a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To scream with laughter is to shriek uncontrollably, so the verb alone can mean helpless, raucous hilarity.

clue.text: See Californian policeman retiring after a revelation

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the letters run backwards
coming after places this run behind the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written
to espy is to catch sight of
Los Angeles, the Californian city
a cop is an informal word for a police officer

explanation.surface: A Los Angeles officer stepping down after some shocking disclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an instruction to the reader but is the first word of the wordplay. Everything from 'See' to 'policeman' is turned round as one run.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocalypse is another name for the Book of Revelation, and the word comes from the Greek for uncovering.

clue.text: Female chasing large, rough Australian marsupial in changing facilities

indicators.note: what chases follows behind, so this piece comes last

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large
an ocker is a boorish, uncultivated Australian
short for kangaroo
Ms is the title for a woman

explanation.surface: A woman pursuing a big, wild kangaroo through a sports club's changing rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: OCKER is Australian slang for a coarse, uncultured man, so 'rough Australian' is one unit, not an adjective plus a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Locker rooms are where people change and store clothes at a gym or sports ground.

clue.text: Warning ladies to give up whiskey

indicators.note: giving something up means letting it go, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: ladies are women
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet; this letter is the one removed

explanation.surface: A caution to women to stop drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'whiskey' spelling points to the NATO alphabet's W, taken from WOMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a sign of something to come, often a foreboding signal that trouble lies ahead.

clue.text: Some highbrow Renaissance architect

indicators.note: 'some' means only a part, so the letters are a portion of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: An intellectual architect of the Renaissance period.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher WREN designed St Paul's Cathedral in London; he was later than the Renaissance, which is only surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Christopher Wren was the English architect who designed St Paul's Cathedral and many City churches.

clue.text: Royal family leads, as if in armour?

indicators.note: what leads goes in front, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: a clan is an extended family
kingly means regal or royal

explanation.surface: The royal family heads a procession, comma and all, before a knightly question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal family' reads as one unit, but it splits, and 'leads' is a verb: the family goes before the royal word. The question mark flags a playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal plates rattle and clank as a knight walks, so moving clankingly is how someone sounds wearing a suit of armour.

clue.text: Fitting carpets, disposing of odd bits

indicators.note: throwing out the odd-numbered positions keeps every second letter

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A carpet fitter clearing away the leftover scraps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitting carpets' reads as the trade, but 'Fitting' is the definition and 'odd bits' means odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Apt means suitable or appropriate, so something fitting for an occasion is apt.

clue.text: Covers rigid creature up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the order flips

blocks.note: set means fixed or hardened
a creature is an animal

explanation.surface: A stiff animal covered over, or a creature that stands up rigid.
explanation.walkthrough: SET + ANIMAL read from the bottom of the light upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To laminate is to cover with a thin protective layer, such as plastic film on a card.

clue.text: Chap seeking to probe apprentice’s financial record

indicators.note: a probe pushes into something, so these letters go inside another word

blocks.note: a cub is a novice, as in cub reporter; the possessive is surface
a chap is a man, referred to as he
a quest is a search

explanation.surface: A man trying to look into a trainee's bank records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeking' reads as a verb but is the noun QUEST; HE + QUEST goes into CUB.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheque stub is the counterfoil left in a chequebook, recording the amount and payee of each payment made.

clue.text: Former Queen Mother supporting upper-class side at Lords

indicators.note: in a down entry, a support sits underneath, so this piece goes below the rest

blocks.note: Q is the abbreviation for queen
U is the old label for upper-class usage
in cricket the on side is the leg side; Lord's is a London cricket ground
a dam is an animal's mother

explanation.surface: The late Queen Mother backing a posh cricket team at Lord's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen Mother' wants to be one royal person but splits in two, with the mother placed beneath U and ON. Lord's is the home of English cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Quondam is a Latin-derived adjective meaning that once was, as in a quondam friend, so it means erstwhile.

clue.text: Try to protect male vanity

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding it, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: to have a pop at something is to try it
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: An attempt to shield men's pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a pop' is British informal for having a go, so a pop is a try.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomp is ostentatious display and splendour, a showy self-importance close to vainglory.

clue.text: Quietly punished errant lover

indicators.note: something punished is knocked about, so the letters are beaten into a new order

blocks.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly
six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An unfaithful lover discreetly chastised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Errant lover' reads as one cheating spouse, but 'errant' is the fodder and 'lover' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A partner is the person one lives with or is romantically involved with, so the word covers a lover.

clue.text: Muse is extremely cool, with heavenly body

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
Io is one of Jupiter's moons

explanation.surface: A goddess of inspiration who is very chic and has a gorgeous figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely cool' sounds like high praise, but it keeps only the ends of the word, and 'heavenly body' sounds like a compliment but is a moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Clio is one of the nine Muses of Greek myth, the one presiding over history.

clue.text: Cleaner is supercilious when cycling

indicators.note: going round in a cycle brings the front letter round to the back

blocks.note: aloof means haughty and distant

explanation.surface: A cleaner who acts snooty while out on a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the A of ALOOF from the front to the back. 'Cleaner' looks like a person but is a bath sponge.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofa is the dried fibrous pod of a gourd, used as a bath sponge for scrubbing skin.

clue.text: Blind German communist regularly missing signage

indicators.note: missing at regular intervals drops every other letter and keeps the rest

blocks.note: a Red is a communist
Herr is the German for Mr
the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A German communist who cannot see, and so misses the road signs.
explanation.walkthrough: A German communist is a Red Herr, so the two words come out in that order. 'Blind' looks like sightless, but it is a noun: a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: A blind is something meant to mislead or conceal, and a red herring is a false clue designed to distract.

clue.text: Cow beginning to disturb female relative

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
an aunt is a female relation

explanation.surface: A cow that starts upsetting a woman in the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' looks like the animal, or an insult, but it is the verb meaning intimidate.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to frighten them into submission, and to daunt is to intimidate or dishearten.

clue.text: Thug loves the curse

blocks.note: a hood is a hoodlum, a gangster
love is zero in tennis, so two loves are two Os

explanation.surface: A gangster who adores swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loves' looks like a verb, but it is plural love, nil in tennis scoring, written as O.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodoo is a run of bad luck or a jinx, something that brings misfortune like a spell.

clue.text: Polish leader of uhlans travelling by train

indicators.note: the leader stands at the front, so only the first letter is taken
things that travel are on the move, so these letters shift into a new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A Polish cavalry commander going by rail.
explanation.walkthrough: Uhlans were Polish and German lancers, which makes 'Polish' look like a nationality; it is the noun meaning refinement.
explanation.definitionFit: Polish here means refined manners, and urbanity is courteous sophistication, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Group of conductors, mostly penniless

indicators.note: most of something is all but a little, so the final letter is left off

blocks.note: bust means broke, with no money left

explanation.surface: An orchestra's conductors who are almost broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductors' suggests orchestras or ticket collectors; it means electrical conductors. A bus or busbar is a set of them.
explanation.definitionFit: In electrical engineering and computing, a bus is a set of parallel wires or conductors carrying power or signals.

clue.text: Rodent biting skin of sportive monkey

indicators.note: the skin is the outside, so only the first and last letters are kept
teeth close around what they bite, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a marmot is a burrowing rodent
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A rodent nipping the hide of a playful monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monkey' sits at the end looking like the victim of the bite, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A marmoset is a small South American monkey with a long tail and silky fur.

clue.text: Force small lock

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests a door, but here it is a curl of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress in physics is force per unit area, and in speech it is the force or emphasis on a syllable.
